title: Questions and doubts
description: A healthy way to ask questions, sit with uncertainty, and avoid online overload.

sections.heading: Questions are part of learning
sections.content: A question is not a spiritual failure. Doubts get heavier when you face them alone or feed them with unreliable sources. The same issue can feel manageable once you have a clear question, a reliable teacher, and a steady routine around it.

sections.heading: Sort the question
sections.content:
Before you search everywhere, work out what kind of question you have:

- Belief: what do Muslims believe, and why?
- Worship: what should I do in prayer, fasting, or purification?
- Emotional: is fear, trauma, loneliness, or anxiety making this feel urgent?
- Source: am I reacting to a claim from an unreliable post or video?

Sorting it first tells you who to ask.

sections.heading: Avoid overload
sections.content: Do not research every difficult topic at once. Pick one question, ask a reliable person, and keep practicing the basics while you wait for an answer. If something you are reading makes you frantic, close it and go back to prayer, sleep, food, and real support.

sections.heading: Ask better questions
sections.content: A strong question includes your situation, what you need to decide, and why it matters. For example: **I am a new Muslim at university, and I am trying to pray Dhuhr between classes. What is the practical beginner option if I only have ten minutes?**

sections.heading: When faith feels flat
sections.content:
The first weeks as a Muslim often feel bright. Later, prayer can feel empty, and you may wonder whether you were ever sincere. A companion named Hanzala felt this. He told Abu Bakr he feared he had become a hypocrite, because the feeling he had with the Prophet faded when he was at home. Abu Bakr said he felt the same. The Prophet told them that if they stayed in that state all the time, angels would shake their hands, and then said three times that there is a time for this and a time for that (Sahih Muslim 2750a).

Another hadith says every deed has a time of zeal and a time of slackening, and there is hope for the person who stays moderate through it (Jami at-Tirmidhi 2453, graded hasan). A feeling is not the measure of your worship. The Prophet said the deeds most beloved to Allah are the regular ones, even if they are small (Sahih al-Bukhari 6464). Sh. Mohammad Elshinawy of the Yaqeen Institute gathers these hadith for the dip after Ramadan, and the same idea fits the dip after conversion.

The psychotherapists Najwa Awad and Sarah Sultan describe a thinking trap called emotional reasoning: "I feel far, so Allah must be far." A feeling is not proof. Comparing yourself with people raised Muslim, or with people online, feeds the same trap.

- Keep the five daily prayers even when they feel empty. Cut back on extras, not on what is required.
- Add one small act you can keep, such as a few verses or one dhikr after Fajr.
- Spend time this week with one practising friend or a class.
- Make dua for a steady heart. The dua page has one.
- Do not decide your conversion was fake, and do not try to fix the feeling with a sudden big programme of extra worship.

A dip in faith and depression can look alike. CAMH says depression may be present when low mood or loss of interest lasts most of the day, most days, for more than two weeks and gets in the way of work, school or relationships. If that sounds like you, talk to a doctor. The mental health page lists where to start.

sections.heading: Am I still Muslim?
sections.content:
Many new Muslims go through a stretch of fearing they have lost their Islam. A horrible thought about Allah comes into their head, they say something wrong, they doubt, or they sin. In a 2025 Yaqeen Institute survey of converts in the United States, 23% said doubts had at some point made them think about leaving Islam. You are not the only one.

**A thought is not a belief.** Some companions told the Prophet (peace be upon him) about thoughts so awful they could hardly say them aloud. He answered, **"That is the faith manifest"** (Sahih Muslim 132a). He also said that Allah forgives the thoughts that pass through a believer's mind, as long as they are not acted on or spoken (Sahih al-Bukhari 2528). Dr. Muhammad Fayez Awad (SeekersGuidance) explains the difference between real doubt and whispers (waswas), and says whispers do not take a person out of Islam.

**What to do when the thought comes.** The Prophet described Satan asking "Who created this? Who created that?" until he asks "Who created your Lord?", and told the believer to seek refuge with Allah and give up such thoughts (Sahih al-Bukhari 3276). In practice:

- Say "A'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim" (I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed devil) and "Amantu billah" (I believe in Allah).
- Turn to something else. Do not argue with the thought, and do not search it online late at night.
- Keep praying. A frightening thought is not a reason to stop worship.

**Sins do not cancel your Islam.** A sin is a reason to repent, not proof that you have left. Feel sorry, stop, and turn back to Allah. The FAQ on repentance, linked below, walks through it.

**Slips of the tongue and forced words.** The Quran excuses someone who is forced to say words of disbelief while their heart is secure in faith, and speaks of leaving faith as willingly opening the heart to disbelief (16:106). Dr. Asim Yusuf, a scholar and psychiatrist writing for SeekersGuidance, puts it this way: **"You can't trip up and stumble out of the religion by mistake; you really have to try!"** He also writes, **"A person who fears not being Muslim is by definition a Muslim."** The detailed rulings are for a qualified teacher, not for a late-night search.

**No need to keep saying the Shahada again.** Repeating it every time a bad thought comes tends to feed the fear. If you are unsure, ask a teacher once and let their answer settle it.

**When it keeps coming back.** Sometimes this fear is part of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which in its religious form is sometimes called scrupulosity. The Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) in Toronto lists "preoccupation with religious images and thoughts or fear of having blasphemous thoughts" among common OCD obsessions, and says treatment ideally combines counselling, most often cognitive behavioural therapy, with medication. Dr. Jibran Khokhar (Yaqeen Institute) writes that thoughts are not sins, and that seeing a qualified mental health professional is **"not a sign of weak faith but a means of healing"**. If the fear takes up hours of your day, talk to a doctor or therapist as well as an imam. The mental health page lists Khalil Center and Naseeha. If the worry is mostly about wudu or prayer, the washing guide has help with whispers too.

This is general information, not medical advice. If you are in danger, call 911. If you are in crisis, call or text 9-8-8.
